implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: wrap the function in an interceptor that derives a canonical key from the argument list, looks that key up in a result store, and on a miss calls the original function, stores its result and returns it. The store carries whatever retention policy the caller can afford - an unbounded map is acceptable only for a small finite domain, otherwise bound it (LRU, TTL, size or weight limit) or key it weakly so entries die with their keys. When the cache is shared, choose the concurrency posture explicitly: unsynchronised (single-owner only), lock-protected (simple, but misses serialize and recursive functions can deadlock), atomic compute-if-absent (one computation per key), or duplicate-tolerant (documented that concurrent identical calls may each compute once). For stampede-prone workloads (many threads or coroutines hitting the same expiring key), layer a singleflight coalescer in front of the memo so exactly one computation runs while others wait for the result. Probabilistic early refresh (XFetch) can also be used to nudge one request to refresh a key ahead of expiry while all others continue serving the stale value.
code_sketch:
memo(f):
    cache = {}
    return lambda *args:
        key = canonical_key(args)
        if key not in cache:              # miss
            cache[key] = f(*args)         # compute once; recursion must reach this cache
        return cache[key]
# shared? add a lock, an atomic compute-if-absent, or document duplicate computation
# stampede-prone? wrap with singleflight: only one computation runs per key at any moment
pitfalls: Memoizing a function that reads mutable state or the clock freezes the first answer for every later caller.
An unbounded store turns the memo into a memory leak in a long-running process; bound it or cap the key domain explicitly.
A key that omits context the result depends on (tenant, locale, configuration version, self) serves the wrong answer with a perfect hit rate.
If the wrapped function recurses through a different path than the wrapper, recursion bypasses the cache and the expected speed-up never appears.

Applying lru_cache to an instance method makes self part of the cache key and holds a strong reference to the instance - the instance can never be garbage-collected as long as any cache entry references it (memory leak on every cached instance method in a long-running process).

Using lru_cache on an async coroutine function: each call returns a new coroutine object; the cache stores the first coroutine without awaiting it, and subsequent callers receive the cached coroutine, which is never re-entered - producing wrong results or silent deadlock.

Cache stampede: when a hot key expires under concurrent load, all N callers miss simultaneously and each independently recomputes, hammering the backing store N times instead of once. Naive lru_cache has no defence; use a singleflight coalescer or probabilistic early expiration (XFetch) in front of the cache.
Synchronized misses serialise all callers on one lock, and if the memoized function recurses through the same cache, it deadlocks on its own lock.
Using a plain dict without a retention policy on a long-running server: memory grows without bound as every unique argument set is permanently retained.

Key collision or equivalence confusion: f(a=1, b=2) and f(b=2, a=1) are separate cache entries (keyword argument order matters); f(tuple([1,2])) and f([1,2]) collide only if the unhashable list is converted first.

TTL jitter: in a distributed system where many processes share a Redis cache, keys with identical TTLs expire simultaneously causing a synchronized stampede wave; adding random jitter to TTLs spreads the expiry window.

Wrong move: use Python functools.cache for an unbounded caller-controlled key domain -> the process retains every distinct argument forever -> instead use bounded functools.lru_cache or an explicit eviction policy.

Wrong move: memoize Clojure or Haskell code that reads mutable or ambient state -> a hit returns a value computed under an obsolete state snapshot -> instead pass the state or version as an argument or clear and rebuild the memo.

Wrong move: assume a memo wrapper makes concurrent misses single-flight -> several callers can compute the same key before the result is stored -> instead add per-key coalescing or atomic compute-if-absent when duplicate work is unsafe.
